newsitem.title: USA: Reader's Digest may hit $40-$50/shr-M. Price.
newsitem.headline: Reader's Digest may hit $40-$50/shr-M. Price.

text.p: Money manager Michael Price said Monday he has accumulated a stake of about 700,000 shares in Reader's Digest Association Inc and sees the common stock selling in the range of $40-$50, if management can turn the troubled publishing group around.
Price, who is chairman of the Franklin Mutual Advisers fund group, said he accumulated the position in the last few months, but had not bought any shares in recent weeks.
Last week, the company said Chief Executive James Schadt resigned and warned that it would lose money in fiscal 1998 as it sought to improve its businesses.

Price said he was drawn to the stock on expectation that the DeWitt Wallace Reader's Digest Fund and the Lila Wallace Reader's Digest Fund, which together own about 72 percent of the company, would reduce their holdings to about 50 percent by the year 2000 to avoid substantial excise taxes.
"They're going to have to find a home for stock," said Price. "They should get the stock up before."
Price said he didn't expect a rapid turnaround. The CEO search will take about two to three months, and the new chief will need about another six months "to get his feet on the ground."
Price said the company has a "fabulous brand name, a great franchise, with great assets in lists and capabilities."
Readers Digest stock rose 9/16 to 27 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange. The company has about 106 million shares outstanding.
On Friday, the company said it hired an executive search firm to help find a new chief executive officer to replace Schadt, 59, who resigned August 11.

The company said August 14 it lost $23 million in the latest quarter as it tried to revamp its businesses, compared with profits of about $46 million a year earlier. The publisher also warned that 1998 results would be weaker than 1997 results.
In 1996, Chase Manhattan Corp merged with Manufacturers Hanover after Price bought a large stake in Chase and helped pressure the bank to improve shareholder value.
